lotl.label: What's Going On With the Leafs
lotl.body: The season died the way too many Leafs seasons do - too many losses, too little margin, and another spring spent staring at the same old unfinished business. Toronto finished 32-36-14, eighth in the Atlantic Division, with 78 points and a season-ending L7; that is not a bad run, it is a flat one, and the standings say it plainly. The headliner is the sign-and-trade for Darren Raddysh, a bold swing that lands a right-shot defenseman and an eight-year commitment worth more than $8 million annually. That move, along with the reports that Toronto was the only club granted permission to speak with Bruce Cassidy and that Jim Hiller's hiring signals a win-now posture, tells you exactly where this organization still lives - chasing urgency, not patience. The problem is the same one that has haunted this franchise for years: the ceiling keeps being promised, but the floor keeps collapsing. Now comes the real test - whether this front office can turn a noisy offseason into a coherent one before free agency and the draft reshape the roster.

lotl.label: What's Going On With the Jays
lotl.body: The Blue Jays woke up with a little swagger and a lot of catching up to do - the kind that comes from a sweep and the hard arithmetic of a 37-38 record. They just finished off the Red Sox with a 4-3 win, capping a three-game sweep and stretching the winning streak to three. That leaves Toronto third in the AL East, 9 games back, but the mood has changed fast from the flat day after the Yankee loss to a club playing cleaner, sharper baseball. Vladimir Guerrero Jr. supplied thunder in Wednesday's 4-3 win, Nathan Lukes kept adding timely pop, and Trey Yesavage - the young arm at the center of the recent buzz - gave them six punchouts and enough calm to keep the sweep alive. That matters because this team has been searching for a run, not a speech. Three straight against Boston gives them one. Now the test is carrying that edge into Wrigley this afternoon against the Cubs at 1:20 PM ET.

lotl.label: What's Going On With the Raptors
lotl.body: The season ended with a tidy record and an unruly to-do list. Toronto finished 46-36, third in the Atlantic Division, and the only thing the final stretch really settled was that this was a good team, not a finished one. The most important recent development is the draft-board scramble around Toronto's options - with Chris Cenac Jr. flagged as a risky swing and guards like Labaron Philon, Cam Carr and Christian Anderson in the conversation. That's the right kind of problem for a club that can afford patience after a year that ended with a 5.0-point margin and 10 games back. The Raptors need more shooting, more stability, and probably one clear answer on the bench or in the room before they start spending real money. RJ Barrett remains part of the long game, which is sensible; the franchise should resist the urge to force a shortcut through a draft class and an NIL era that keep reshuffling value. Toronto has earned the right to be selective, even picky. Now comes the real test - picking the right prospect, protecting the cap, and turning a respectable 46-36 into something sturdier next season.

lotl.label: What's Going On With the Commanders
lotl.body: The quiet work of June is where a team's paint starts to dry - and Washington's got a fresh coat on the defense, with Daronte Jones already shaping the new edges of the room. Odafe Oweh and K'Lavon Chaisson stood out at minicamp, a useful sign for a club that finished 3rd in the NFC East, 6 games back, with a season that ended 1-0 and left no illusion about the gap to the top. The real story now is not last fall's record; it's whether these additions can turn a front seven that has been redesigned in the image of Dan Quinn's staff into something nasty enough to matter. Oweh brings speed off the corner, Chaisson brings the kind of springy, prove-it energy that can change a practice field in a hurry, and both arrive with a chance to win snaps before the pads even come on. Washington has spent all spring talking about fit, not flash. What matters next is whether that minicamp juice survives into training camp, when depth charts stop being suggestions and start becoming law.
